sources.quote: a ten day cooling off period, a one year maximum term, no automatic renewal without the consumer agreeing
sources.title: Joining a gym or fitness club
sources.evidence: If you sign a membership contract that requires you pay $50 or more in advance you are protected under the Consumer Protection Act. You have the right to cancel a membership within 10 days of receiving a written copy of your contract. All contracts must end after one year. Contracts may be renewed only if the gym follows certain rules, including sending you a renewal notice at least 30 days, but not more than 90 days before the contract expires.

sources.quote: bar automatic renewal, require instalments rather than money up front, and require a permit and security from the Office de la protection du consommateur
sources.publisher: Office de la protection du consommateur (Québec)
sources.title: Contents of the Contract and Terms of Payment – Fitness and Weight Management Centres
sources.evidence: Any clause that allows the merchant to renew automatically is prohibited. The total amount of the invoice must be paid in at least 2 approximately equal instalments claimed at regular intervals. Fitness and weight management centres must have a permit from the Office de la protection du consommateur; to get this permit, the centre must provide a deposit to the Office.

sources.quote: ten days to cancel after receiving a copy, a twenty four month ceiling including renewals, and further rights if a member moves away
sources.title: Fitness or personal services contracts - rules for businesses - Consumer Protection BC
sources.evidence: Continuing services contracts can't exceed 24 months and after that, the membership must move to a month-to-month term. Consumers can cancel within 10 days of getting a copy of the contract for any reason, and can cancel if there have been certain types of changes in the circumstances of the customer or in the services provided (called a material change), such as relocating more than 30 km away from the facility.

sources.quote: is drip pricing, which amendments passed in 2022 addressed expressly
sources.title: Drip pricing - Competition Bureau Canada
sources.evidence: In 2022, the Government of Canada amended the Competition Act to explicitly recognize drip pricing as a deceptive business practice. The amendments confirm that representing a price that a customer cannot actually attain because there are mandatory fixed additional charges or fees is a false or misleading representation (subsections 52(1.3) and 74.01(1.1)). This does not apply to charges or fees that are entirely government imposed.

sources.quote: prohibit ads that generate negative self perception
sources.title: Health and Wellness - Meta Transparency Center
sources.evidence: Ads must not imply or attempt to generate negative self-perception or declare that there is a perfect body type or appearance one should aspire to in order to promote diet, weight loss, cosmetic procedures or any other health-related products. Ads must not contain side by side imagery depicting before and after weight loss/gain not related to the use of a product or service.

sources.quote: kinesiologist is protected in Ontario under the Kinesiology Act, 2007
sources.title: Did you know your title is protected? – College of Kinesiologists of Ontario
sources.evidence: In Ontario, only COKO registrants can practise kinesiology, call themselves Kinesiologist and Registered Kinesiologist and use the designations R.Kin and R.Kin (Inactive). These titles and designations are protected under the Kinesiology Act, 2007, which states that no person other than a member shall use the title kinesiologist, a variation or abbreviation or an equivalent in another language.

sources.quote: Ontario's Consumer Protection Act, 2023 is expected to replace the 2002 Act
sources.title: Business guide to consumer protection
sources.evidence: In 2023, the Ontario government introduced a new Consumer Protection Act, which when it comes into effect, will renew and update Ontario's consumer protection laws. Until then, the existing Consumer Protection Act, 2002 (CPA), remains in effect.

sources.quote: with markedly predominant French on public signage since June 2025
sources.publisher: Office québécois de la langue française
sources.title: Entreprises : affichage des marques de commerce et des noms d'entreprises
sources.evidence: New rules concerning public signage and commercial advertising, particularly regarding business names or trademarks, have been in effect since June 1, 2025. For French to be markedly predominant in signage, the French text must occupy a space at least twice as large as text in another language and have permanent character with visibility and readability at least equivalent to any other language text.
